Title: Capabilities Imprint: A Graph-Theoretic Framework for Transport Infrastructure-Based Capabilities Evaluation
Authors: Sangeeta, Rui Teixeira, Hrishikesh Dev Sarma, Helen McHenry, Beatriz Martinez-Pastor
Abstract: This paper introduces the Capabilities Imprint , a novel conceptual and quantitative Capability Approach (CA) to assess how spatially embedded infrastructure enables individual human capabilities. The framework models dependencies on essential infrastructure and amenities using transport networks and allows for graph-theoretic metrics to quantify individual capabilities through their imprints. The premise of this approach is that, from a CA perspective, each person is at the centre of a network of infrastructure and amenities that has a role in the potential of that person to achieve the life they value, and this is their Capabilities Imprint . This imprint can then be quantified using network theory through metrics such as Connectivity Scores (CS) and Betweenness Centrality (BC), enabling an understanding of the transport infrastructure context for individuals. CS quantify access to key amenities, while BC identifies critical nodes within the imprint, whose disruption would disproportionately affect multiple capabilities. In this work, capabilities are conceptualized as locational, focusing on domain-specific infrastructural and spatial conditions that shape opportunities through transport network connectivity and integrity. A case study in Swords, Ireland, demonstrates the methodological implementation of the Capabilities Imprint framework and its ability to generate actionable insights for planning and policy. Clustering analysis of connectivity profiles reveals distinct community archetypes, highlighting areas facing systemic infrastructure exclusion. Simultaneously, high-betweenness nodes pinpoint network bottlenecks, informing prioritization for planning or further action. The approach also captures overlapping dependencies across capabilities, showing how failures at a few critical junctures can cascade through multiple facets of urban life. The framework relies on open-source data and a two-metric approach combining accessibility and network vulnerability, enabling a spatially disaggregated and network-aware assessment of infrastructure-enabled capabilities. In doing so, the Capabilities Imprint supports equity-oriented spatial analysis and accessibility-informed urban planning, offering policymakers a practical tool for human well-being–centred decision-making and more just prioritization in urban transport planning.

Title: Infrastructure remembers: network continuity and the making of divided Jerusalem, 1943–1962
Authors: Shlomi Efrati
Abstract: How does a city’s public transit network withstand the shocks of political partition, mass immigration, and the redrawing of international borders? Urban history has traditionally marginalized public transportation as a passive background rather than an active driver of a city’s spatial evolution. To address this gap, this study reconstructs the bus network of the Jewish HaMkasher cooperative — the city’s dominant urban operator from 1931 until its absorption into Egged in the 1960s — across two pivotal snapshots: 1943, under late British Mandate rule, and 1962, in the divided city, when the network was confined to the western sector. The reconstruction draws on a previously unexplored corpus of primary documents from the Egged Archives (which hold the HaMkasher records) and the Jerusalem Municipality Archives, including 1943 distance tables, a 1962 cartographic map, and detailed administrative records from the District Motor Regulatory Board. Methodologically, this archival data was georeferenced and transformed into line-level graphs, ultimately creating unified network models for both time periods. By computing both degree and betweenness centrality for every stop, the study maps the underlying structural roles within the network. A null-model comparison preserving each stop’s arrivals and departures shows that the resulting concentration of brokerage on the western corridor reflects the historical configuration rather than the reconstruction’s topology. Furthermore, the severe disruption of the 1949 armistice line provides analytic leverage for weighing infrastructural inertia against the persistent geographic constraints of Jerusalem’s mountainous terrain and its fixed commercial core. The findings reveal a continuity beneath the era’s dramatic geopolitical ruptures. Long before the 1948 partition, the Jaffa Road corridor already functioned as a pivotal structural bridge. Rather than forcing a total reorganization of the transit system, the Armistice Line activated vulnerabilities already latent within it. Consequently, the post-1948 westward expansion relied on this preexisting corridor, and the grafting of new immigrant neighborhoods onto the system quantitatively manifested as arrested polycentrism. Ultimately, this research demonstrates that the spatial logic of a transit infrastructure can outlast — and quietly constrain — the profound political and demographic transformations of the city it serves.

Title: The impact of information intervention and carbon credit incentive on fostering green travel behaviour: A behavioural experiment study in Shenzhen, China
Authors: Yinlian Zeng, Fengni Chen, Lijun Gao, Lei Gong, Lina Wang
Abstract: Fostering green travel behaviour among commuters is an important approach to reducing transport-related carbon emissions. This study examines how information intervention, differentiated by rational information (RI) versus emotional information (EI), combined with carbon credit incentives, influence green travel choices among private car owners in Shenzhen, China. Drawing on the framing theory (FT) and the theory of planned behaviour (TPB), this study develops a conceptual framework that links information intervention with behavioural decision-making pathways. Difference-in-differences and generalised structural equation modelling were applied to app-based commuting data and post-intervention survey measures. RI and RI combined with carbon credits (RICC) were associated with significant reductions in car commuting, whereas EI was not statistically significant, and EI combined with carbon credits (EICC) showed only marginal significance. Post-estimation comparisons indicate that the difference between RI and EI was not statistically significant, while the difference between RICC and EICC was marginally significant. Carbon-credit treatments generated larger negative point estimates than their corresponding information-only treatments, but their incremental effects were not statistically distinguishable. Generalised structural equation modeling indicates that the interventions were associated with behavioral change through attitude, perceived behavioral control, environmental concern, and behavioral intention, whereas the subjective norm pathway was comparatively weak. These findings suggest that rational information may align more closely with routine commuting decision criteria than affective appeals in the short term. It also indicates that, under the tested implementation conditions, app-based carbon credits did not generate statistically distinguishable behavioral gains beyond information provision alone. The study contributes by applying the FT framework to real-world commuting interventions and linking behavior effect estimates with psychological pathway analysis.

Title: Ranking critical bridges in wide-area road networks through iterative macroscopic traffic simulation
Authors: Amirehsan Charlang Bakhtyari, Francesco Deflorio
Abstract: Bridge failures in case of disruptive events can lead to severe mobility interruptions and losses in regional connectivity. This study proposes a scalable and computationally efficient network modeling methodology to support the prioritization of bridge monitoring and retrofitting under resource constraints by integrating publicly available datasets, hazard information, and simplified incremental macroscopic traffic simulation. Using Alessandria, Italy, as a case study, baseline and disrupted road network scenarios were generated, where flood-exposed bridge edges were iteratively closed one at a time to represent flood-induced disruptions. An origin–destination matrix was estimated to assess traffic redistribution under each disruption scenario. Traffic performance indicators were then used to quantify the impacts of bridge-edge closures on regional mobility, and the analysis was extended to complete physical-bridge closures. The findings reveal that while local bridges may produce high relative increases in travel time, motorway bridges generate disproportionately large absolute impacts due to their high traffic volumes, underscoring their crucial role in maintaining regional connectivity. The principal criticality patterns were preserved when complete physical bridges were closed, while comparison with a topological assessment highlighted the importance of considering traffic demand and route redistribution. A traffic-demand sensitivity analysis further confirmed the robustness of the identified critical bridges under variations in motorway crossing demand.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Strategic regulation of human-machine traffic: a Stackelberg framework for low-carbon policy design
Authors: Yicheng Zhang, Zelin Wang, Qian Liu, Zheyi Yang, Zhiyuan Liu
Abstract: Reducing carbon emissions from urban transportation remains a critical challenge. With the rapid advancement of intelligent technologies, connected and autonomous vehicles (CAVs) offer significant potential for promoting low-carbon mobility. This study proposes a Stackelberg game framework to capture the human–machine interactions among government-regulated CAVs and privately operated human-driven vehicles (HVs) and autonomous vehicles (AVs), which is formulated as a bilevel optimization problem. To address the computational challenges in urban-scale transportation networks, a mixed block coordinate descent (MBCD) algorithm is proposed to enable parallel solution of the lower-level traffic assignment problem. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the multi-threaded MBCD algorithm achieves up to an 8 × speedup when utilizing 10 threads on two real-world networks. Further experiments reveal that among the three vehicle types, CAVs contribute the most to emission reduction, followed by AVs, while HVs are identified as the primary source of carbon emissions. A transportation system composed entirely of CAVs can reduce fuel consumption and CO 2 emissions by about 9%-15% compared to a fully HV system. Further analysis shows that optimal fuel efficiency is achieved when the volume-to-capacity ratio reaches approximately 0.7 on both tested networks, whereas both free-flow and heavily congested conditions result in higher fuel consumption per mile.

Title: Modelling of public transport route choice adaptations to unplanned metro disruptions using smart card data
Authors: Lawrence Christopher Duncan, Benjamin Cottreau, Ouassim Manout
Abstract: It is vital that public transport disruption mitigation strategies are supported by a clear understanding of travel behaviour and preferences, including of disrupted route choices. This paper, for the first time, uses smart card data to analyse multimodal public transport route choices immediately after being disrupted by an unplanned metro service closure while en route. We develop methodologies for identifying commuters and their usual commute route, approximating home/work locations, and identifying disrupted trips and onward post-disruption routes. These methodologies are operationalised in a case study of Lyon, France, where 5031 post-metro-disruption routes are identified, including routes taking bridging buses (bus replacement services). These route observations are used to estimate a multimodal route choice model with a detailed utility function that provides good fit to the data. Route choice preferences and behaviours are analysed and compared with those from usual commute route choices. Some of the key findings are that, post-disruption: there is a stronger dispreference for transferring and a lower dispreference for in-vehicle time, metro is less innately attractive than bus/tram, contrasting with usual commuting preferences, bridging bus is the least innately attractive mode, users have a stronger dispreference for egress time than access time (from the disrupted metro), and there is a positive preference for route robustness. Results are also compared with those from existing studies, impacts of disruptions on travel times are evaluated, and policy implications of the work are discussed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Network motifs reveal mobility disruption during Hurricane Ian
Authors: Zeyu He, Yujie Hu
Abstract: Understanding how natural disasters reshape daily mobility is essential for improving preparedness and strengthening community resilience. This study develops a motif-based analytical framework to quantify mobility disruption during Hurricane Ian in Lee County, Florida, using high-resolution smartphone location data. Daily mobility motifs are constructed at the individual trajectory level and classified by their relationship with inferred home locations, distinguishing home-anchored, home-passing, and non-home mobility structures. Motif changes are then aggregated to the census block-group scale to examine spatial disparities through canonical correlation analysis, clustering, and ordinal logistic regression. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity across both motif types and neighborhoods. Within Lee County, Hurricane Ian weakened home-anchored routines, increased home-only and non-home mobility, and produced sharper contractions in simple motifs relative to more complex ones. At the community scale, home-anchored disruption was primarily associated with household composition, education, age structure, and commuting patterns, while non-home motif increases were more strongly linked to geographic exposure, population density, local service proximity, and income conditions. By capturing both routine contraction and disruptions to home anchoring across scales, this study demonstrates a motif-based approach for examining mobility disruption in a severe hurricane context and provides a common analytical basis for comparative applications across geographies and disaster types.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Measuring perceived long-distance accessibility
Authors: Milan L. Moleman, Bert van Wee
Abstract: Over recent years, perceived accessibility has gained interest, yet is primarily studied in the context of daily travel. Relatively little is known about perceived long-distance accessibility, that is, the perceived ability to reach distant destinations of at least 100 km away. This paper develops and tests a measurement scale for perceived long-distance accessibility using data collected in 2025 among long-distance travellers in the Netherlands. First, we conduct an exploratory factor analysis to identify the underlying factors of perceived long-distance accessibility. Next, we apply a confirmatory factor analysis to validate the factor solution. Lastly, we explore relations between perceived long-distance accessibility levels and background information (among others, gender, age, educational attainment, employment status, household income, and level of urbanity) using a linear regression model and latent class analysis. Our analysis reveals four key dimensions of perceived long-distance accessibility among Dutch long-distance travellers: travel options, digital skills, needs and desires, and time availability. Overall, the measurement scale developed in this paper allows to quantitatively identify differences in levels of perceived long-distance accessibility among individuals, which in turn equips policymakers and practitioners with insights necessary to promote a more inclusive long-distance passenger transport system.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Designing transport systems for people with non-visible disabilities
Authors: Chu Shi Qi Chloe, Mikela Chatzimichailidou
Abstract: The accessibility and inclusivity of transport systems are critical to promoting health, equity, and participation, and require an understanding of the experiences and diverse needs of all users. Persons with disabilities, who are recognised as vulnerable road users, face elevated transport risks and increased challenges in navigating transport environments, often resulting in reduced accessibility and participation. Among them, individuals with non-visible disabilities experience compounded challenges, arising not only from the functional limitations of their impairments, but also from social and systemic obstacles due to the unseen nature of their conditions. Despite this, mobility studies specifically focusing on non-visible disabilities – conditions in which impairments are not outwardly apparent – remain limited and fragmented, often confined to condition-centric studies. This scoping review aims to identify the barriers and impacts experienced by individuals with non-visible disabilities when using transport systems, and to highlight key considerations for future interventions. Three non-visible disabilities – autism, dementia, and anxiety disorders – were selected to guide the literature search and analysis. Findings reveal the heterogeneity across the three selected conditions, along with common mobility barriers such as confusion and complexity in transport systems, and the overwhelming nature of the travel environment. Consequently, individuals across the three selected conditions often modify their travel behaviour and reduce social participation. The review identifies key principles for inclusive design, including people-centric planning, systemic integration of support and training, and an emphasis on actionable design changes to create accessible environments.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Fare evasion strategies, perceived safety, and travel choices in public transport: evidence from a vignette experiment
Authors: Benedetto Barabino, Martina Carra, Jérémy Celse, Roberto Ventura
Abstract: Fare evasion poses persistent challenges for public transport systems, with implications for financial sustainability, social norms, corporate image, and perceived safety and security. While deterrence strategies such as increasing inspection frequency or fine severity are widely used, their effects on passengers’ perceptions and behavioural spillovers remain weakly evidenced. This study examines how anti–fare evasion cues influence travel preferences, perceived safety and security, and fare‐evasion intentions, accounting for time of day and competition from a ride‑sharing service (RSS). Four research questions were examined through a vignette‑based randomised experiment. Participants chose among a non‑manipulated bus route, a manipulated route (enforcement or service cue), and an RSS alternative across seven conditions crossing enforcement cues (inspection, fines, neutral) and period (day/night). The results showed that the effects of anti–fare evasion cues were small and statistically uncertain. Neither inspections nor fines produced clear improvements in perceived safety or security (RQ1), and the enforcement type showed no consistent direct effect on the choice of the manipulated route (RQ2). Night-time conditions did not meaningfully change safety or risk perceptions, nor did they reliably moderate the association between perceived route safety and route choice (RQ3). Fare evasion was more frequent at night and less frequent on the manipulated route yet contrasts between Fine and Inspection treatments remained small and imprecisely estimated (RQ4). The RSS garnered only 3.73% choices amid price differentials. Thus, deterrence failed to bolster reassurance or ridership proxies, with choices driven by safety and security perceptions independently of cues. Night primarily led to increased evasion without corresponding gains in safety and security. Policies should pair targeted enforcement with service enhancements, particularly nocturnal, in multimodal contexts.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Underestimation of the costs of owning and running a car
Authors: Adam Joachim Shier, Shane Timmons, Peter D. Lunn
Abstract: Car ownership and use appears less responsive to cost increases and income declines than might be expected, a pattern often attributed to habit formation and lifestyle adjustment. An additional explanation is that motorists may underestimate how much they spend on owning and running a car, but there is little empirical evidence testing this possibility. Using a representative sample of 801 motorists, we compare intuitive estimates of the annual motoring costs with detailed itemised expenditure across all major fixed (e.g., tax, insurance) and variable (e.g., fuel/charging, parking) costs over the same period. Total reported costs are almost 50% higher than motorists intuit. Median intuitive costs were €2,000, while median itemised costs were €2,923, excluding purchase price and depreciation. Most motorists (over 70%) exhibit this underestimation bias, with similar rates across engine types and socio-demographic groups. These findings are consistent with recall failures and salience bias when motorists consider the costs of owning and running a car, with potential implications for the persistence of car ownership. Improving the visibility and aggregation of motoring costs may complement fiscal and infrastructural measures aimed at supporting sustainable modal shift.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Windows of change as precursors to changing travel behaviour aligned with sustainable mobility
Authors: David A. Hensher, John D. Nelson, Edward Wei, Thiranjaya Kandanaarachchi, Camila Balbontin, Chinh Ho, Corinne Mulley, Wen Liu
Abstract: There is an increasing focus on ways in which we can achieve behavioural change associated with improved sustainability outcomes in the transport sector. In societies where the car is the dominant passenger transport mode with all of its associated interpretations of convenience, we continue to search for ways to change travel habits that result in a switch out of the car in favour of public transport and active modes. Beyond the existing research on mobility biographies, this study proposes the concept of “Windows of Change” (WoC), representing the cycle of key events driving travel behaviour changes of individuals. The study demonstrates that WoC works in ways that support sustainability outcomes. We categorise the WoC into four broad classes: lifestyle and household changes (e.g., changes in living arrangements, family structure, or personal habits); work and commuting-related changes (e.g., changes in employment, workplace incentives or commuting patterns); transport and mobility changes (e.g., changes in vehicle ownership, public transport use or travel habits); and social and environmental considerations (including awareness and influence of others). In particular, the study applies a series of negative binomial count models to identify the relationship between the key events in WoC and modal one-way trip frequency in a typical week associated with the WoC period, after controlling for various socioeconomic effects and country dummy variables. Data is collected from over 4,000 respondents spread across Australia, Finland, New Zealand, the United States, the United Kingdom, Singapore, and Sweden, investigating respondents’ local travel behaviour changes over the period 2023–2025, showing the concept of WoC can be applied across countries and cultural contexts. The findings provide a rich array of policy advice on what key WoC influences suggest actionable ways to support the switch to more sustainable modes, and what remain as clear barriers to achieving such an outcome.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Exploring road users’ perceptions of fatbikes and riders’ behaviours in the Netherlands: Implications for public acceptability
Authors: Soyeon Kim, Dennis Andreoli, Marjan Hagenzieker
Abstract: Fatbikes, electric fat-tire bicycles, are increasingly visible in the Netherlands. Although fatbikes are classified within the broader electric bicycle (e-bike) category, fatbikes may be perceived as a distinct and riskier mobility mode than conventional e-bikes. As this perception can affect public acceptability, it creates a challenge for their integration into urban mobility systems. Yet empirical evidence on the perceptions and acceptability of fatbikes remains limited. This study examines Dutch road users’ perceptions of fatbike riders and their behaviour, and how these perceptions are associated with the public acceptability of fatbikes, based on an online survey of 508 respondents. Results show that fatbike riders are perceived negatively, often associated with youth and reckless riding behaviour. Compared to regular e-bike riders, fatbike riders are viewed as engaging more frequently in traffic violations and unsafe behaviours. Public acceptability of fatbikes is also considerably lower than that of e-bikes, which are perceived more neutrally. Interestingly, public transport and scooter users are more likely to view fatbikes as an alternative mode of transport. These findings suggest that policy responses need to address the behaviours and concerns that shape acceptability, rather than focus solely on the vehicle category. Policy implications, therefore, include behaviour-focused measures, such as enforcement and education to promote safe riding and prevent illegal modifications, as well as public information campaigns that clarify lawful and safe fatbike use. This study contributes to ongoing discussions on new mobility by providing empirical evidence and policy guidance for safer, more sustainable urban transportation.
