Title: Will high-speed rail compete for long-distance travel in a car-dependent society? Insights from a Canadian high-speed rail survey
Authors: Yu (Billie) Zhang, Ahmed El-Geneidy
Abstract: High-speed rail (HSR) represents a significant transport investment designed to drive economic growth and enhance long-distance regional connectivity. While HSR has demonstrated strong competitive performance against road and short-haul air travel in European and East Asian corridors, the behavioural parameters governing how HSR competes against the private vehicle in automobile-oriented North American markets, where car travel accounts for over 80% of intercity trips, remain comparatively underexamined. It is therefore less clear how travellers in such markets weigh travel time, cost, and service quality when a mature HSR alternative is introduced into a car-dominated mode share structure. The goal of this paper is to evaluate the potential for modal shift to HSR within the structural constraints of a car-dependent society. Unlike studies in transit-integrated European or Asian contexts, this study isolates the group travel penalty and car-habituation effects that characterize North American intercity travel. The study uses the Toronto-Québec City corridor in Canada, which was announced as an HSR project in 2025, to better understand if such investment can achieve its intended ridership and sustainability targets. The study analyzes data from an online bilingual long-distance travel behaviour survey (N = 6,813) conducted in October 2025. We develop a two-stage sequential weighted multinomial logit model capturing current travel behaviour and stated HSR adoption intentions. The analysis reveals that travellers are most sensitive to travel cost and travel time, with an implied value of travel time of approximately $31.5 per hour. Under a medium-adoption scenario, HSR is projected to capture 26% of corridor trips, with the largest substitution from private car and conventional rail. These findings provide an evidence-based demand projection that is essential for investment decisions while avoiding the common pitfall of ridership overestimation in large HSR projects. Practitioners can use these insights to prioritize fare-based incentives and target specific trip purposes such as business and student travel, to maximize the operational success of future HSR projects.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Cooperative drone-based hitchhiking vehicle framework for last-mile logistics services: A case study for online food delivery scenarios
Authors: Zijian Ding, Fan Zhang, Wei Ma
Abstract: The rapid advancement of low-altitude technology has shown significant potential to revolutionize the traditional ground-based last-mile logistics services. However, technical and operational challenges (such as limitations on payload size and weight, as well as battery capacity restrictions) hinder the widespread adoption of drone-based logistics systems, which can be addressed by a cooperative vehicle-drone delivery approach. In view of this, we investigate the drone-vehicle cooperative delivery problem through a multi-layered architecture that formally synchronizes urban transit networks, drone distribution systems, and logistics operations. To be specific, we propose the drone hitchhiking last-mile delivery framework (DHLDF) to enhance urban last-mile logistics services. To facilitate the framework's deployment, a decentralized agent-based heuristic is developed to operationalize the DHLDF through real-time spatio-temporal coordination. The proposed approach is validated through a high-fidelity simulation of Manhattan's urban fabric, synthesizing real-world taxi trajectory datasets with commercial food-delivery demand. Experimental results demonstrate that DHLDF significantly enhances systemic throughput, achieving a 20.6% improvement in success rates and an 11.9% reduction in energy consumption compared to direct drone delivery by achieving higher drone turnover rates. Moreover, case studies conducted on real-world urban networks demonstrate the practical applicability of DHLDF in diverse last-mile delivery scenarios. These findings offer meaningful insights for policymakers and logistics managers regarding the operational efficiency, scalability, and adaptability of DHLDF to complex spatial-temporal demand patterns, highlighting its potential for real-world implementation.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Evaluating urban rail transit vulnerability: A link-centric framework integrating network connectivity and passenger accessibility
Authors: Yun Wang, Rufan Yang, Yunqiao Xiang, Mingfang Yuan, Yu Zhou, Xuedong Yan, Xing Chen
Abstract: Understanding how disruptions reshape network structure and generate heterogeneous accessibility losses is essential for vulnerability assessment in urban rail transit (URT) systems. This study develops a unified link-centric framework that jointly examines disruption-induced structural changes and passenger accessibility consequences under multi-scenario settings. Disruption scenarios are constructed using an interval-based representation that captures structural dependencies under turn-back constraints, ensuring realistic propagation patterns. Passenger impacts are evaluated through an OD-level accessibility classification based on feasible paths and detour thresholds, distinguishing unaffected, partially affected, and fully affected OD pairs. These components are integrated through a composite link-importance indicator that couples network topology with demand distribution, enabling identification of structurally critical and functionally consequential links. The framework links structural fragility with passenger outcomes, supporting more realistic identification of critical links based on structural dependency and accessibility loss. Application to the Beijing URT network shows that vulnerability is concentrated in the southwestern corridor, particularly along the Fangshan Line and southern Line 9, where disruptions cause significant accessibility losses. Targeted structural interventions effectively mitigate impacts, as adding a connection in the vulnerable corridor reduces fully affected OD pairs from 10,565 to 2,470. Sensitivity analysis confirms the stability of identified vulnerable regions under different penalty factors, while validation in Shenzhen and Nanchang demonstrates the framework's transferability across systems with varying sizes, topologies, and demand patterns. This study provides a unified, demand-sensitive framework linking structural disruptions with accessibility outcomes, offering practical guidance for resilience-oriented URT planning and emergency management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Accelerating electric vehicle adoption in India: A System Dynamics approach considering purchase and charging infrastructure subsidies
Authors: Mahavadi Dhanshyam, Ashish Srivastava, Alok Raj, Prateek Bansal
Abstract: Policymakers worldwide increasingly view faster adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) as an important pathway to reducing transport-related greenhouse gas emissions. However, EV adoption is shaped by interactions among various stakeholders and by a range of economic, technological, infrastructural, and perceptual factors. To examine this dynamic process, we develop a System Dynamics (SD) model comprising five interlinked modules—the Vehicle Adoption Dynamics Module, EV Utility and Market Share Module, Cost and Market Evolution Module, Charging Infrastructure Module, and subsidy module that considers two policy levers: a purchase subsidy and a charging infrastructure subsidy. Using India's EV market as the empirical setting, we examine the relative effectiveness of these two policy instruments under 14 scenarios. Our results show that under the Business-as-Usual scenario, adoption is initially driven by affordability and later by convenience, especially through reduced range anxiety and improved service support. While purchase subsidies generate stronger short-run gains by overcoming the early affordability barrier, their marginal impact declines over time, and they impose a higher fiscal burden. In contrast, charging infrastructure subsidies are more cost-efficient, producing stronger long-run adoption gains by improving charging availability, reducing range anxiety, and supporting ecosystem development. Overall, a phased composite policy mix performs better than both standalone interventions and extreme front-loaded support, indicating that early affordability support combined with sustained infrastructure investment is the most effective and fiscally prudent strategy for accelerating EV adoption. These findings offer practical guidance for policymakers designing EV-promotion strategies that are both effective and fiscally prudent.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Longitudinal evaluations of the coverage and pricing differences between transportation network companies and traditional taxis: A case study of New York city
Authors: Hanyong Xu, Jinhua Zhao
Abstract: App-based ride-hailing has expanded and operated alongside traditional street-hail taxi services for the past decade, both competing with and complementing one another. This evolution raises questions about how the two systems compare longitudinally in pricing and coverage. This study provides an empirical analysis of seven years of trip records from New York City, examining spatial and temporal differences between Transportation Network Companies (TNCs) and traditional taxis. It highlights how their comparative dynamics have evolved, particularly during major shocks such as the COVID-19 pandemic and congestion pricing policy. First, the study applies trip count Log Ratios, Shannon's Entropy, the Gini Index, and counterfactual fare estimation to show that TNCs offered wider, more consistent coverage and a more pronounced price surge than taxis during the pandemic. Second, it introduces a composite typology based on fare differences and relative coverage, revealing a gradual shift toward a TNC-dominated market. Third, a spatial lag panel model with random effects, controlling for trip attributes and built environment, uncovers associations between neighborhood characteristics and the service differences between TNCs and taxis. In general, comparing before and after the pandemic, neighborhoods with more car-less households experience fare gaps reversing and TNC trips surpassing taxis, while neighborhoods with more minorities saw lower TNC fares and growing TNC share. These findings underscore the need to establish ongoing monitoring frameworks, foster competitive markets, move beyond simplistic trade-offs, address spatial disparities in algorithmic pricing, and recognize systematic change in behaviors for long-term planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: From early adopters to the mass market: policy implications of heterogeneous value of time in drone delivery
Authors: Doosun Hong, Eunhyang Lee, Tao Feng, Sunghoon Jang
Abstract: As drone delivery emerges as a solution to strained urban freight systems, successful implementation requires navigating the complex trade-offs between logistical efficiency and public acceptance. This study investigates the determinants of consumer adoption and estimates the heterogeneous Value of Delivery Time (VoDT) to inform policy and service design. Using a web-based stated choice experiment in Seoul, South Korea, we analyze the impact of level-of-service attributes alongside critical operational constraints, including weather, noise, and autonomy, as well as social influences. A hybrid latent class mixed logit model segments consumers into “early adopters” and “late adopters” based on their attitudes toward innovation. The results reveal a stark behavioral divide: early adopters, driven by novelty, exhibit a high willingness to pay for speed (particularly for electronics) and tolerate operational uncertainties. In contrast, late adopters, the mass market, are risk-averse, highly sensitive to noise above 70 dB, and deterred by negative social reviews. We estimate VoDT ranging from 1.49 to 9.92 USD per hour, varying significantly by adopter class and commodity type. These findings suggest that a “one-size-fits-all” regulatory approach is insufficient. Instead, policymakers and planners must manage a transition from permissive frameworks facilitating early adoption to strict reliability and noise standards required for mass societal acceptance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: How can drivers be nudged to avoid distracted driving? The effects of nudging risk type and density through a serial mediation of arousal level and perceived risk
Authors: Yang Liu, Pengkun Wu
Abstract: The high frequency of traffic accidents underscores the crucial importance of warning drivers against distracted driving, particularly during the autonomous driving process. Although extant studies on distraction mitigation have delved into distraction sources and distraction detection, they have mostly neglected the effectiveness of nudging content and density, as well as the underlying mechanisms that influence driver responses. Grounded in Nudge Theory and Situated Action Theory, this study investigates how the nudging risk type and density impact driver responses to distraction prompts through a serial mediation of arousal level and perceived risk. It also examines the moderating effects of road weather conditions. Through three experiments, this study demonstrated that immediate risk exerts a stronger influence than potential risk in shaping drivers’ responses. Additionally, higher nudging density, which reflects both greater stimulus intensity and a shorter inter-stimulus interval, is associated with more favorable driver responses. Nudging risk type influences driver responses only through a sequential mediation pathway involving arousal level and perceived risk, while nudging density has both direct and indirect effects via the same mediating mechanism. Under rainy conditions, the effect of nudging risk type on arousal level is attenuated, and the effect of nudging density on driver response is likewise diminished. This study makes a theoretical contribution to the literature on information nudges in driving scenarios.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Editorial Board
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Corrigendum to “A novel network equilibrium model integrating urban aerial mobility” [Transp. Res. Part A 187 (2024) 104160]
Authors: Honggang Zhang, Zhiyuan Liu, Yu Dong, Hongyue Zhou, Pan Liu, Jun Chen
Abstract: The authors regret an inaccurate statement in Proposition 2 and in two related summary sentences of the published article. The LAC-NE formulation is a convex optimization model and admits at least one optimal link-flow solution. However, the convexity argument establishes that the Hessian matrix is positive semidefinite, rather than positive definite; hence, strict convexity cannot be concluded and the optimal link-flow solution is not necessarily unique. Accordingly, the statements claiming “uniqueness” should be revised to refer to the existence of an optimal solution. In addition, two minor typographical errors were identified in Section 4.2 and Section 5. In Section 4.2, ''AGI-NE model'' should read ''LAC-NE model''. In Eq. (33), the summation used to update the flow on the shortest path should be taken over the non-shortest paths of the same OD pair, rather than over all OD pairs. This correction clarifies the OD-wise flow conservation used in the path-based gradient projection update and is consistent with Eq. (27) and the algorithmic procedure described in the paper. These corrections concern only the statement and conclusion regarding uniqueness and the two typographical issues noted above. The derivations establishing the convexity of the LAC-NE model remain valid, apart from the final inference of uniqueness. The corrections do not affect the mathematical formulation of the LAC-NE model, the solution algorithm, the numerical examples, or the other conclusions of the article. The authors would like to apologise for any inconvenience caused.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The impact of digitalization on accessibility: an introduction
Authors: Joris Beckers, Elnert Coenegrachts, Ahmed El-Geneidy, Karst Geurs
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Tracks of equality: high-speed rail and its effects on intra-regional inequality—a quasi-experimental study based on China’s district/county-level data
Authors: Jiahao Lai, Fan Zhang, Ruilin Luo, Guo Chen
Abstract: The efficacy of high-speed rail (HSR) remains controversial, with critics contending that its welfare disproportionately accrues to affluent demographics, potentially exacerbating inequality. In this study, we employ nighttime light data at the district/county level in China from 2000 to 2019 to construct a nighttime light inequality index as a proxy for intra-regional inequality. Utilizing a quasi-experimental approach (Difference-in-Differences), we investigate the impact of HSR implementation on intra-regional inequality in China. We find that HSR significantly reduces inequality along its routes, with districts/counties experiencing mitigation of local disparities primarily through three channels: technological innovation, entrepreneurial activity, and urban expansion. HSR's inequality-reducing effects are most pronounced in megalopolis with multiple centers and balanced structural layouts. The presence of national-level tourist attractions enhances HSR's mitigating effect on local inequality. Notably, red tourism sites associated with Chinese Communist Party history exhibit a more substantial augmenting impact on HSR's inequality-reducing effects compared to conventional tourist attractions. Our research findings contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the welfare effects of HSR and offer policy implications for developing nations contemplating HSR as a means to alleviate poverty and stimulate economic growth.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The impact of purchase subsidy termination on electric vehicle adoption: a synthetic control approach
Authors: Carsten Creutzburg, Leo M. Doerr
Abstract: This study provides the first real-world evidence on the effects of an unanticipated termination of Battery electric vehicle (BEV) purchase subsidies in Germany, one of the world’s largest BEV markets. We exploit the abrupt, court-mandated termination of Germany’s subsidy program in December 2023 as a natural experiment and analyze the causal impact of this exogenous policy shock by applying the Synthetic Control Method to monthly BEV registration data from January 2018 to March 2025. Our estimates suggest that the German BEV market declined by approximately 45% as a direct result of the subsidy termination, corresponding to 140,000 BEV registrations that were forgone in 2024 alone. Our findings underscore the critical role of financial incentives in promoting BEV adoption, while also highlighting the importance of clear communication and predictable policy timelines, as abrupt changes pose substantial risks to market stability, decarbonization targets, and government credibility.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Comparing public investments across sectors with CBA-based impact information and participatory budget choices
Authors: John M. Rose, Andrea Pellegrini
Abstract: This paper proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates cost–benefit analysis (CBA) with participatory budgeting (PB) to inform public-sector portfolio choices. To highlight the approach, we assume that CBA has been conducted to evaluate twelve independent infrastructure and service projects, establishing their economic viability. Subsequently, PB is employed to elicit community preferences regarding the same projects, ensuring alignment with public values. The combined framework aims to reconcile technical efficiency, understood here as welfare-economic appraisal implemented through standard modelling and valuation conventions, with democratic legitimacy, captured through direct, budget-constrained citizen prioritisation. Our findings show that respondents gave the strongest average support to health care and utilities projects, with education also performing relatively well, while public transportation and road infrastructure were preferred to transport-electrification initiatives. In contrast, public projects associated with private vehicle and freight vehicle electrification attracted comparatively weak support, and public transportation electrification was supported less strongly than conventional public transport investment. More broadly, respondents tended to favour projects that delivered larger consumer-surplus and environmental benefits and projects located in, or relevant to, their own area.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Evaluating local-area transport interventions through mobile phone GPS data: a framework and case study of low traffic neighbourhoods
Authors: Xianghui Zhang, Peter Jones, Andy Emmonds, Tao Cheng
Abstract: There is increasing adoption of local-area transport interventions worldwide, as part of a strategy to encourage more sustainable mobility. However, the impacts of such interventions are complex and wide-ranging and often difficult to monitor using conventional instruments, as they include various travel modes (e.g. car, bus, cycle, and walk), different population groups (e.g. residents, visitors, and non-local travellers), and multiple scales of influence (both social and spatial). This paper presents a new comprehensive evaluation framework to assess local-area scheme interventions that leverages the continuous, high-granularity spatial coverage of mobile phone GPS data to overcome these limitations. This framework is then applied to examine the impact of a set of Low Traffic Neighbourhood (LTN) Schemes in North-East London, in which through traffic is removed from predominantly residential areas, using road closures and traffic filters. Using Propensity Score Matching and a Difference-in-Differences model, it explores issues related to changes in mobility and activity patterns, at both individual and spatial levels. The findings reveal that, in this sample of LTNs, residents have reduced their driving outside LTNs and spend more time walking and engaging in other activities within their LTNs. It also enhances local attractiveness, as evidenced by increased footfall among non-residents during weekdays. Moreover, in this case the LTNs have reduced motor traffic flow on both internal and surrounding roads, challenging the notion that traffic is merely displaced to closely adjacent main roads. However, the LTNs have resulted in former pass-through drivers taking longer routes, potentially transferring motor traffic and increasing road usage in surrounding residential areas. This study demonstrates the value of using mobile phone GPS data and causal inference methods to provide a broader and richer evaluation of local-area transport interventions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Environmental impact of a green tax on new vehicle sales in the presence of tax exemptions
Authors: Andrés Gómez-Lobo, Juan José Price
Abstract: At the end of 2014 a “Green” registration tax on new vehicle sales was introduced in Chile. In this paper we use a vehicle registration dataset to estimate the impact of this policy on average nitrogen oxide (NOx) emission rates of new vehicle purchases. We analyze two impact channels: substitution from diesel to gasoline vehicles and substitution from more to less polluting models within each fuel class. We rely on a difference-in-differences approach and focus our analysis on pickup trucks. Our identification strategy benefits from the fact that for this type of vehicle the policy defined a taxable and exempt group. In addition, the tax was increased on two occasions after its implementation, hence we can estimate its impact as a function of treatment intensity. Our findings suggest that an average tax that reached 7-8% of the sale price resulted in an overall increase of 4 to 8 percentage points in the probability of purchasing a gasoline over a diesel pickup truck for affected purchases, reducing the average emission rate for this class of vehicles. In addition, we find suggestive evidence that within the diesel pickup group the tax may have induced a substitution to a cleaner model once it became available in the market. The policy's aggregate environmental impact is small since a large fraction of the most polluting vehicles are exempt. Finally, we do not find evidence of an increase in CO2 emissions as a result of the tax. Policy recommendations are discussed.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Penalties as prices? evaluating airline strategic responses to tarmac delay penalties in the US
Authors: Hideki Fukui, Martin Dresner, Chikage Miyoshi
Abstract: We examine whether penalties for lengthy tarmac delays in the US aviation industry deter such incidents or are instead regarded by carriers as an acceptable cost of doing business. Exploiting penalties imposed on marketing carriers for severe-weather tarmac delays as a quasi-natural experiment, we compare changes in taxi-out and taxi-in times, the rate of lengthy tarmac-delay incidents, and cancellation rates between penalized and non-penalized carriers using difference-in-differences and synthetic difference-in-differences estimators. We find modest improvements in operational performance following penalties but also observe, in several cases, no improvements or even adverse changes. Specifically, the deterrent effect of these penalties seems to weaken when they are small relative to carriers’ net incomes. Our results suggest that current penalties provide only limited deterrence and may be perceived by some carriers as an everyday cost of doing business, especially when financial conditions are favorable.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Understanding the influence of public transport perceptions on the adoption of demand responsive transport services in the UK: A case study
Authors: Shobhit Saxena, Chiara Calastri, Christine Currie, Julia Bennell, Rym M’Hallah
Abstract: This study investigates the adoption potential of demand-responsive transport (DRT) services in a large UK urban region, with particular emphasis on the role of perceptions toward existing public transport (PT) infrastructure. While DRT is often promoted as a sustainable alternative to conventional modes, its urban implementation in the UK has yielded mixed results, partly due to a limited understanding of behavioral factors that influence its uptake. We employ a hybrid modelling framework combining revealed and stated preference data from 1,490 respondents in the Greater Leeds region, integrating latent perceptions of PT reliability, safety, connectivity, and affordability within a random utility maximisation structure. Unlike traditional integrated choice and latent variable (ICLV) models, we adopt a parsimonious specification using a single-indicator approach, facilitating better interpretability and policy simulation. Our analysis indicates that PT perceptions significantly influence modal preferences, with improvements in safety and connectivity increasing the likelihood of DRT adoption. Notably, these findings challenge the prevailing notion of DRT as a competitor to PT, instead emphasising the complementarity between the two modes. Our policy simulations demonstrate that a balanced “carrot-and-stick” approach--one that simultaneously improves PT infrastructure and service quality while discouraging private car use—can strengthen perceptions of PT, increase its ridership alongside DRT, and ultimately support a modal shift away from private vehicles.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Hydrogen-powered aviation: What do we know and where do we go?
Authors: Zahra Jaffary, Yahua Zhang, Zhifang Wu, Kun Wang, Xiaowen Fu, Yifei Cai
Abstract: The transition to hydrogen-powered aviation is a critical step toward achieving net-zero emissions in the aviation industry. However, significant uncertainties and research gaps remain in understanding its feasibility, deployment and broader implications. This literature review analysed 138 hydrogen-related articles published between 2015 and 2025 to assess the current state of research. The synthesis included the lead authors and their affiliations, the citations, the status of the leading journals and highlighting key thematic areas. The key thematic areas identified include carbon reduction policies, hydrogen-powered aircraft, the hydrogen supply chain and infrastructure, safety and the environmental impacts of hydrogen fuel in aviation. An understanding of these thematic areas is essential for shaping future research priorities, particularly in areas such as airport hydrogen demand, supply chain and infrastructure planning, and policy frameworks. The findings of this literature review can offer valuable insights for airports, airlines, policy makers, decision makers and hydrogen industries in supporting the uptake and offtake of hydrogen fuel. Based on our findings, we call for (1) in-depth airport-specific case studies to assess hydrogen infrastructure needs, comparing onsite, offsite and hybrid supply chain models in particular; (2) an investigation of demand profiles at airports as well as spatial constraints and the feasibility of hydrogen development; and (3) the identification of the supportive policy frameworks and regulatory measures that will be required to enable a successful transition to hydrogen power at the airport level.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Urban informal transportation and gentrification: empirical evidence from motorcycle taxis in Bangkok, Thailand
Authors: Shota Emoto, Daniel del Barrio Alvarez, Prasongchai Setthasuravich, Saksith Chalermpong, Phathinan Thaithatkul, Muhammad Zudhy Irawan, Hironori Kato
Abstract: This study investigated the role of informal motorcycle taxi services in shaping residential and commercial gentrification patterns around rail stations in Bangkok. Although Transit-Oriented Development (TOD) has been widely associated with displacement and spatial inequality, limited research has examined how informal transportation systems intersect with these processes in the context of the Global South. Through propensity score and Mahalanobis distance matching with stratified analysis, this study estimates the average treatment effect of motorcycle taxi presence on gentrification outcomes across 250-m and 500-m rail station buffers. Although the baseline results revealed no significant citywide effects, the stratified analyses revealed geographical heterogeneity. First, in inner-city, transit-rich areas, motorcycle taxi presence is positively associated with both residential and commercial gentrification, suggesting that these services may reinforce accessibility-driven redevelopment. In contrast, in peripheral areas with limited transit coverage, motorcycle taxis mitigate residential gentrification by enhancing the mobility of low-income residents and supporting informal agglomerations. Second, in areas at medium distances from rail stations, motorcycle taxi presence was linked to increased commercial gentrification and decreased residential gentrification. Third, motorcycle taxis have significantly positive associations with commercial gentrification in areas of older rail stations but insignificant in those of younger rail stations. These patterns reveal the dual and context-sensitive role of informal transportation in urban transformation. This study contributes to debates on informality, accessibility, and gentrification in Global South contexts and calls for TOD frameworks to incorporate informal mobility systems as both infrastructural assets and tools for inclusive urban development.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Impacts of transportation infrastructure on the stopping behavior of heavy commercial vehicles
Authors: Jishi Wu, Tao Feng, Peng Jia, Gen Li, Junyi Zhang
Abstract: Restricting heavy commercial vehicles (HCV) stopping behavior is essential for traffic management and efficient logistics organization. However, insights into HCV stopping behavior conditional on infrastructure remain limited. We utilize large GPS HCV trajectory data to investigate the spatial variability of stopping duration and its associated influential factors. Results show HCV stopping duration and pre-stop trip distance exhibit marked weekday-weekend heterogeneity, with longer stops and longer preceding trips being more likely to occur on weekdays. We further propose a spatial random forest model to predict HCV stopping duration. In addition to the superiority of the proposed model, we found parking distribution and land use collectively contribute to 76.76% of the predictive power, with trip distance identified as the most influential factor, followed by distance to the nearest freight rail station and to the nearest port, respectively. Furthermore, the analyses also exhibit complex non-linear associations between influential factors and stopping duration, and significant threshold effects. These findings offer valuable insights that can serve as a nuanced guide for planning HCV parking management.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Public preferences for transport infrastructure improvements: An analysis of attitudinal drivers
Authors: Friederike Beck, Michiel C.J. Bliemer, Allister Loder
Abstract: Research has shown that public support for transport policy measures is one of the key factors affecting the successful implementation. But the heterogeneity in the population for broader policy objectives , namely the prioritisation of improvements across transport modes, had rarely been examined in detail. But understanding public preferences for transport policies is crucial for designing politically feasible pathways towards sustainable mobility. This study investigates how attitudes, socio-demographic/economic attributes, mobility behaviour, and built environment characteristics shape preferences for infrastructure improvements across modes. After administering an online stated ranking survey ( N = 2 , 011 ) , we conducted an exploratory factor analysis to identify latent attitudinal dimensions and estimate a three-class latent class rank-ordered logit model. Results reveal five distinct attitudinal factors and three heterogeneous preference classes: environmental enthusiasts (18.82 %), car pragmatists (34.18 %) and moderates (47.00 %). Environmental attitudes emerge as a central cleavage that influences preferences for general infrastructure improvements across different modes. Furthermore, respondents’ own mobility patterns strongly shape preferences, highlighting a pronounced self-interest bias. We find that moderates , representing almost half the sample and exhibiting a balanced attitudinal profile, could be a receptive group for targeted interventions, where increased exposure to sustainable modes may further strengthen their support for related policies. These findings suggest that reframing investments in sustainable transport to emphasise accessibility and service quality may enhance public support for policies aligned with decarbonisation goals.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A welfare-based evaluation framework for UAVs in last-mile delivery: economic assessment and roadmap design
Authors: Xing Yao, Yaru Li, Chunan Wang, Bowen Yi, Ying Fan
Abstract: As a disruptive logistics delivery solution, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is now transitioning from conceptual model to practical application. Its large-scale deployment will influence social welfare across multiple dimensions, rendering it an issue that cannot be overlooked in policy formulation. This study establishes a welfare analysis framework for last-mile delivery, systematically comparing UAVs with traditional ground vehicles in terms of cost, efficiency, and externalities. By aggregating these components, the study evaluates net welfare impact resulting from the transition in last-mile delivery methods. The analysis identifies delivery distance, labor wages, and battery costs as major factors affecting welfare of utilizing UAVs in last-mile delivery. Based on an analysis of 31 provinces in China, regions with higher labor wages and short delivery distances are more suitable for prioritizing the promotion of UAV logistics. Applying a net welfare gain criterion for substituting traditional ground vehicles with UAVs in last-mile delivery, this study projects that 24 out of 31 provinces in China will be ready for large-scale adoption of UAV delivery by 2035. This highlights the 2030–2035 period as a strategic policy window for promoting UAV delivery. Based on estimates using 2024 express delivery volumes, this transition will bring China net welfare gains of 3.96 billion USD by 2030 and 26.30 billion USD by 2060. However, this transition is accompanied by increased energy consumption and emissions, which calls for close attention from policymakers.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Impact of real-time crowding information on mass-transit passengers’ platform placement choices
Authors: Florian Leprévost, Arthur Portron, Kirusha Krishnakaran, Élise Grison, Simone Morgagni
Abstract: Crowding in public transport systems affects both passenger comfort and network efficiency. Besides operational solutions, interventions targeting passenger behaviour could address this issue efficiently. Real-Time Crowding Information (RTCI) systems, which display coach-level occupancy on platform screens, can help passengers avoid the most congested coaches or trains. However, existing research on RTCI's impact on passenger behaviour, relies predominantly on stated preference surveys, where respondents declare a single dominant strategy. Such designs cannot capture the trade-offs passengers make when competing cues – entrance proximity, exit knowledge, and crowding information – simultaneously influence their choice, nor can they reveal dynamic effects arising when passengers confront actual crowding after receiving RTCI. Here, using two online behavioural experiments – a schematic click-map task (N = 186) and an active snapshot navigation task (N = 397) – we quantified how passengers integrate these competing placement cues into hybrid positioning strategies. We found RTCI massively shifted positioning away from crowded coaches (79–91%), but crowd avoidance did not function as an independent strategy: it emerged only when crowding conflicted with a preferred position, producing compromise behaviours. For instance, when both exit and crowding were near the entrance, 63% of participants positioned themselves just past the crowded zone, to remain close to the entrance and exit. Additionally, the crowding level indicated by RTCI also modulated passengers’ reaction to actual on-board density upon train arrival: at equivalent real density, passengers who had been shown a high-crowding signal on their platform zone were significantly more likely to make a last-minute coach change, suggesting that RTCI sets expectations that amplify perceived crowding. These findings demonstrate that behavioural measures reveal a complexity of positioning strategies that stated preference approaches can miss. This has direct implications for the design and deployment of RTCI systems, as unanticipated passenger redistribution and rushed platform behaviour must be accounted for to ensure operational efficiency.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Unraveling systematic and unobserved heterogeneity in willingness-to-pay for traffic safety improvement: A hybrid decision tree and latent class Tobit approach with evidence from Pakistan
Authors: Fazle Subhan, Hongmei Zhou, Muhammad Asif Khan, Shengchuan Zhao, Huanhuan Luo, Van Duy Tran
Abstract: Evaluating traffic safety initiatives through cost-benefit analysis is essential for policymakers seeking effective resource allocation, and understanding individuals’ willingness-to-pay (WTP) for improved traffic safety has therefore garnered increasing attention in recent years. However, important challenges remain in modeling WTP, namely, (i) the absence of systematic higher-order interactions in models, resulting in omitted variable bias and inaccurate model inferences, and (ii) the use of conventional models that presume a constant impact of explanatory variables on WTP, overlooking unobserved heterogeneity. This study addresses these gaps by integrating a decision tree with a latent class Tobit (LCT) model. The decision tree identifies potential systematic higher-order interactions that serve as inputs to the LCT model. The LCT model captures unobserved heterogeneity by partitioning individuals into distinct classes and identifying class-specific factors. The proposed modeling framework is tested on a sample of 653 car drivers from Peshawar, Pakistan. Results reveal two distinct classes in the population: “high” and “low” financial contributors. They further show that variables not significant in a conventional Tobit model become significant in different classes of the LCT model. Higher-order interactions identified through the decision tree are also incorporated in the model, capturing systematic heterogeneity in preferences. In addition, WTP for fatal and severe injury risk reductions is estimated and used to calculate the corresponding risk-reduction values. Overall, the proposed modeling framework enhances understanding of individuals’ sensitivities toward WTP for improved traffic safety and provides actionable insights for policymakers seeking to target distinct population groups.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: How our values and means shape optimal transit fare policy
Authors: Tianxing Dai, Yu (Marco) Nie
Abstract: This study examines how optimal fare policies are shaped by the need to balance moral values and financial means. Motivated by the growing interest in fare-free transit (FFT) and the lack of rigorous modeling frameworks to evaluate its impacts, we develop a joint transit design model that incorporates a means-based step-fare structure encompassing full-fare-free (FFF), partial-fare-free (PFF), and standard-discount-fare (SDF) policies. The model accounts for behavioral responses such as the zero-price effect, as well as operational and administrative savings from eliminating fare collection. It is then employed to identify optimal fare policies under both utilitarian and egalitarian objectives across a range of financial scenarios. Applied to the case of Chicago, our analysis yields several key findings. First, optimal policies depend critically on funding levels: FFF is both egalitarian and utilitarian only when robust financial support is available. Second, contrary to common belief, a utilitarian is more likely than an egalitarian to support FFF, as equity goals often require targeted benefits. Third, increasing financial flexibility does not always lead to more publicly acceptable designs. These findings offer guidance for transit agencies navigating the post-pandemic fiscal landscape and planners pursuing more sustainable and equitable urban mobility for their communities.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Two-region mixed autonomy network with park-and-ride: Macroscopic modeling, microscopic validation, and multi-scenario analysis
Authors: Yifan Li, Ziyuan Gu, Nan Zheng, Wei Ma, Zhiyuan Liu
Abstract: Urban transportation networks often face severe congestion and parking difficulties during peak periods due to demand–supply imbalances in traffic and parking. Park-and-ride (P&R) policies have been widely adopted to mitigate these issues by diverting vehicles to parking facilities near the boundary between central and outer regions of the city. However, the emergence of autonomous vehicles (AVs) fundamentally reshapes traffic dynamics and parking behaviors, thereby challenging the effectiveness of traditional transportation management polices. This study proposes a parsimonious two-region mixed autonomy network (MAN) model that incorporates self-driving-and-parking AVs and P&R dynamics to analyze their combined effects and mutual influences. The model is built upon an extended multi-pool representation tailored to MANs and employs an accumulation-based approach to capture the dynamic evolution of different vehicle families within the system. Discrete choice models and Monte Carlo simulation are further integrated to characterize the distinct parking behaviors of AVs and human-driven vehicles (HVs). The consistency analysis against a microscopic model confirms that the proposed macroscopic model accurately captures the temporal evolution of traffic network conditions. Additionally, experimental results demonstrate that while P&R remains effective for regulating HV inflow to central regions, its impact diminishes as AV penetration increases, owing to AVs’ ability to self-park. These findings suggest that AV-specific management policies may be required to complement traditional HV-oriented P&R strategies. Overall, the proposed model offers a structured approach to inform decision-making on various urban parking policies and services for better traffic management in the era of AVs.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A quantitative framework for assessing rail station operational resilience under infrastructural modifications
Authors: Md Tabish Haque, Jan Eisold, Nikola Bešinović
Abstract: Rail stations are critical components in rail networks, shaping both operational continuity and urban connectivity. The station area, comprising station platforms, throat, and immediate approach segments with dense concentrations of routing and control elements, makes it highly susceptible to disruptions. While prior research has largely focused on network-level resilience or examined station resilience through the lens of passenger-infrastructure interaction, the role of traffic-infrastructure interaction within station areas in maintaining operational stability remains under explored. This study introduces an optimization-based resilience assessment framework that examines how the spatial configuration within station areas can mitigate disruption impacts and enhance operational performance. The approach evaluates the influence of localized infrastructure modifications on station operational resilience. A real-world case study from the German rail network demonstrates the framework's applicability. Results indicate that although resilience is highly sensitive to disruption characteristics and traffic density, targeted infrastructure modifications can significantly reduce overall impact, constrain deviations, and support faster recovery across diverse disruption scenarios. Further, the study highlights that during severe disruptions involving multiple simultaneous failures, targeted infrastructure modifications continue to have better performance, supporting service continuity. The findings support infrastructure managers to assess on resilience improvements with reference to infrastructural modifications and taking informed decisions.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Digital twin federation for urban mobility assessment: Definition, pillars, and a human-in-the-loop functional architecture
Authors: Jingjun Li, Jascha Grübel, Ali Nadi, Maaike Snelder, Bart van Arem, Jie Gao
Abstract: Urban mobility systems face growing challenges. While various smart mobility solutions have been proposed, there is still a lack of comprehensive tools for assessing the impact of these solutions in a dynamic and iterative manner. Recent literature increasingly adopts the Digital Twin (DT) concept. However, DTs have conventionally been framed around automating solutions, which often conflict with the requirements of human-driven planning in socio-technical systems, leading to ambiguities in how DTs should be defined and operationalised for mobility planning. To fill this gap, this paper presents the concept of a Digital Twin Federation (FedDT) designed for comprehensive urban mobility assessments. Firstly, a definition of the FedDT concept is established based on four conceptual pillars, including physical & digital system exchange, system monitoring & planning, outcome evaluation & immersive experience, and human-in-the-loop control. Building on the concept and 5 stakeholder co-design sessions, we present a functional FedDT architecture that enables iterative, bidirectional data exchange between the physical and digital mobility systems, thereby supporting a data-driven decision-making process while ensuring the interests of stakeholders are continuously integrated. Finally, we demonstrate how the FedDT architecture can be instantiated through a proof-of-concept application framework. This framework serves as a research agenda that guides and links the development of separate modules to reduce private vehicle dependency in Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Overall, this work lays a conceptual and architectural foundation for FedDT, advancing the implementation of integrated digital twin solutions for sustainable mobility systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Consumer involvement in last-mile e-commerce transport and impact on travel Patterns: A case study in Sweden
Authors: Lena Winslott Hiselius, Emeli Adell, Ulrik Berggren, Lena Smidfelt Rosqvist
Abstract: The growth of e-commerce has transformed consumer shopping patterns and reshaped travel behaviour, yet knowledge is limited regarding how different delivery options interact with individual mobility in everyday life. This study analysed how delivery options, trip characteristics, and socio-demographic and spatial factors relate to e-commerce activity travel and the degree of consumer involvement in last-mile transport . Using a longitudinal, smartphone-based travel survey combined with daily reporting of e-commerce activities, data were collected. The dataset prepared for analysis included 238 respondents, validating 11,221 days and 48,145 trips. Of these, 197 respondents engaged in an e-commerce activity at least once in a 28-day period. The results showed that nearly 60% of e-commerce activities required out-of-home travel, indicating substantial consumer involvement in last-mile logistics. Many of these trips were conducted as standalone errands, particularly for deliveries collected from agents and delivery boxes. Delivery boxes and in-store pickups were associated with car usage for e-commerce travel, while trip chaining facilitated integration of the pickup into broader activity patterns and mode use. Socio-demographic characteristics (including age and car access) and frequency of e-commerce use significantly shaped travel mode and delivery choices, with frequent users of e-commerce showing lower car dependence. Spatial context further moderated behaviour: urban residents displayed greater use of in-store pickups and other modes than cars, whereas rural residents depended more on cars. Overall, the findings demonstrate that e-commerce does not replace physical mobility, but reshapes it in ways dependent on delivery design, trip context, and local setting.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: The distributional effects of high-speed rail investment in China: fast tracks to inequality?
Authors: Xutao Yang, Erik Verhoef, Mark Lijesen, Jianhong Wu
Abstract: High-speed rail (HSR) has become one of China's most ambitious infrastructure projects, redefining accessibility and connectivity across vast regions. However, rigorous empirical investigations on the impact of HSR on the conventional rail (CR) operation and the following effects on CR passengers remain scarce. Therefore, we investigate how CR trips, often made by low-income groups, are impacted by the operation of HSR using a comprehensive rail operation dataset. Our regression discontinuity design (RDD) results reveal that the operation of HSR leads to a significant decrease in CR trains (CT) frequency with both immediate and sustained declines observed, and slows down the increase of travel speed over the years. Heterogeneous impacts are found in different travel station types, different types of CT, and HSR operation intensity. Our imputed effects indicate that aside from construction and operation cost by using the public investment, the distribution of benefits and costs on CR passengers is overall regressive, since the generalised cost changes appear to benefit high-income groups, but disadvantage low-income groups.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Household life-cycle heterogeneity in commuting to emerging subcenters: An excess commuting-based study of the Seoul metropolitan Area, South Korea
Authors: Hyunseong Yun, Seung-Nam Kim
Abstract: New employment subcenters are continuously emerging in global metropolitan areas. The growth of employment in emerging subcenters attracts workers from a wide range of areas, potentially leading to extremely long commuting distances. Many emerging subcenters primarily comprise high-tech industries, which are more favorable to workers in younger life cycles. Subcenter studies encourage planners to supply an adequate quantity of housing to keep jobs and housing balanced in order to mitigate attracted commutes. However, the effects of the job-housing balance on attracted commutes to emerging subcenters require investigation, because the heterogeneity of emerging subcenters raises concerns regarding spatial mismatch across household life cycles. This study aims to provide evidence that a quantitative job-housing balance may contribute to mitigating attracted commutes by examining commuting behavior in the Seoul Metropolitan Area, South Korea, across household life cycles. Utilizing Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP)-minimized employment data from 2006 and 2016, seven Traffic Analysis Zones are identified as emerging subcenters. Excess commuting indices are measured to demonstrate inter-life-cycle heterogeneity in the relationship between the job-housing balance and observed commuting behavior. Cross-classified multilevel analysis indicates that commuting distance is shorter when commuters live in locations with greater nearby job opportunities and work in locations with greater nearby residential opportunities. Together with observed commute comparisons and multilevel model results, the findings suggest that quantitative job-housing balance may help moderate attracted commutes to emerging subcenters.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A two-level collaborative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for variable speed limit control of freeway tunnel groups
Authors: Jieling Jin, Hui Zhang, Lu Xing, Helai Huang, Yansheng Chen
Abstract: Compared to freeway mainline sections, freeway tunnels present a higher risk of collisions and pose greater challenges for rescue operations, owing to the distinctive features of tunnel lighting and structures. Moreover, the safety demands for tunnel groups, which consist of multiple tunnels, are more pronounced. Recent studies have demonstrated the promising application of reinforcement learning in implementing variable speed limit (VSL) control on freeways to enhance safety and efficiency. However, existing approaches cannot adequately capture the interaction of traffic flows across different tunnels in group scenarios, nor can they efficiently train policies under highly complex environments. This study proposes a VSL strategy based on a two-level collaborative multi-agent reinforcement learning (TCMARL) framework to improve the safety and efficiency of freeway tunnel groups. The framework realizes coordinated control at two levels: (1) capturing potential spatial dependencies among tunnel agents through a spatial graph model, thereby achieving synergy at the information input level; and (2) constructing a mixing network that fuses features of different tunnel agents and introducing an importance weight vector to optimize the global Q-value output, achieving synergy at the action output level. To improve training efficiency and policy generalization, a model-based reinforcement learning mechanism is further incorporated to generate short-horizon virtual rollouts. Simulation experiments are conducted in four tunnel-group scenarios, including two-, three-, four-, and five-tunnel configurations. Comparative results show that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and better safety and efficiency performance than benchmark methods. Additional ablation and sensitivity analyses confirm the complementary roles of the two-level collaboration design and the model-based planning mechanism, while out-of-training testing under unseen demand profiles demonstrates robust transferability. Beyond algorithmic performance, the findings provide policy relevant evidence for corridor level speed management in smart freeway tunnel systems, informing practical guidelines on coordinated VSL deployment and operational governance.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: A multi-source, multi-stage framework for ride-hailing safety management
Authors: Jiayu Yang, Jaeyoung Jay Lee, Suyi Mao, Constantinos Antoniou
Abstract: The rapid growth of ride-hailing services has transformed urban mobility, but the predominance of non-professional drivers raises pressing safety concerns. Existing research often lacks a comprehensive framework that integrates trajectory, environmental, and driver-related data to thoroughly examine risky driving behaviors. To address this gap, this research proposes a framework to analyze, predict, and intervene in speeding and jerky driving among ride-hailing drivers. It also explores the underlying factors contributing to such behaviors and offers targeted improvement strategies. The analysis uses a rich multi-source dataset, including over six million GPS trajectories, OpenStreetMap road network, and real-time weather data, along with 450 self-reported questionnaires from ride-hailing drivers. A multi-stage framework is employed, consisting of three components: (i) a bivariate random parameter model with heterogeneity in means to identify contributing factors to risky driving behavior; (ii) a Dual-Task Gated Cross-Attention Network for real-time risk prediction and proactive safety monitoring; (iii) a Gradient Boosting Classifier model to investigate factors influencing drivers’ willingness to reduce risky behaviors. The analysis illustrates that, while speeding and jerky driving share common risk factors, such as trip distance and acceleration, they diverge substantially in their sensitivity to infrastructure and geometric conditions. The questionnaire survey analysis reveals several factors that influence a driver's willingness to improve their behavior: driving experience, driver ratings, risk perception, income level, and crash history. Overall, the proposed framework offers a robust, data-driven approach for managing risky driving in ride-hailing services, supporting real-time supervision and targeted policy development to enhance urban road safety.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Transport substitution and travel resilience under bad weather: evidence from high-speed rail and air travel in China
Authors: Xinlei Hu, Shuping Wu, Longfei Zheng
Abstract: The growing frequency of extreme weather events presents challenges for transportation resilience. The substitution of different travel modes can enhance travel resilience under bad weather conditions. Using a novel dataset of nearly 3.7 billion high-speed rail (HSR) booking records in China from 2014 to 2016, this study estimates the extent to which HSR services are a substitute for air travel during bad weather conditions. Combining a difference identification strategy with high-dimensional fixed effects, we find that 2% of HSR trips (approximately 1.827 million trips) traveling over two hours can be attributed to air trips shifted to HSR during bad weather conditions. This weather-induced substitution is more pronounced for 2–7 h HSR trips and occurs mainly on weekdays and long holidays. The resilience of HSR to bad weather has generated welfare gains of approximately 151.61 to 400.13 million RMB for intercity travelers during 2014–2016.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Bridging land use and transport planning: An AI-enabled decision support system for new urban developments
Authors: Jiawei Tong, Guangyu Wang, Ruoxi Liao, Shuihua Wang, John Moraros
Abstract: Rapid urban expansion demands immediate land use decisions whose transport implications shape accessibility for decades. Yet traditional approaches lack transparent mechanisms to link controllable planning features (density regulations, network design standards, zoning policies) to observable mobility consequences, breaking the connection between what planners can control and what they need to predict. To address this fundamental challenge, we introduce Adaptive Dynamic Analysis for Predictive Transport (ADAPT), an explainable AI framework employing a two-stage architecture: Stage One learns categorical traffic patterns from 4397 established scenarios using conditional variational autoencoders, revealing that functional classification explains 38% of variance while density and spatial context contribute 28%. Stage Two transfers learned patterns to new developments through intelligent initialization and online adaptive learning. ADAPT advances land use-transport integration by linking planning features to observable mobility patterns through interpretable prediction. It provides three capabilities: feature importance estimates that show which planning characteristics predict traffic generation, context-dependent mechanisms that identify nonlinear thresholds across urban forms, and uncertainty-aware protocols that align infrastructure commitment with prediction confidence. Validated across 663 new development scenarios in three metropolitan areas (Los Angeles, San Diego, Tokyo), ADAPT achieves 17.9–35.1% performance improvements over state-of-the-art baselines while enabling evidence-based planning from initial approval stages.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: How does shipping alliance affect port capacity investment and congestion
Authors: Tianyu Shang, Hao Wu, Dong Yang, Chuan Zhao, Kun Wang, Changmin Jiang
Abstract: This study investigates the economic implications of alliance formation, focusing on port capacity investment as the critical channel affecting congestion and social welfare. We identify two potentially countervailing mechanisms governing the port's investment incentives: the market effect, where economies of scale boost throughput and encourage investment; and the congestion-relief effect, where improved vessel coordination alleviates port congestion but may crowd out investment. Our findings reveal that while the net impact of the shipping alliance on investment depends on the relative strength of these forces, port congestion consistently decreases due to the alliance's operational efficiency. Furthermore, although alliance formation improves total social welfare through direct efficiency gains, it does not resolve the structural inefficiency of the market: port capacity investment consistently remains below the socially optimal level. To address this distortion, we characterize the optimal capacity subsidy policy. We demonstrate that when alliance coordination acts as a substitute for capacity investment, the private incentive to invest weakens further, necessitating higher government subsidies to align private investment with the social optimum.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Investigating usage intentions for MaaS over time: A stage-based lens considering pre-adoption, onboarding, and post-adoption stages
Authors: Zuoxian Gan, Ting Liang, Ruijia Zhao, Yunting Song, Tao Feng
Abstract: Previous studies have primarily examined the individual stages of MaaS use intention, overlooking the fact that user acceptance is an evolving, multi-phase process. Moreover, while most existing studies focus on pre-adoption intentions regarding MaaS, fewer examine its initial use, and even fewer investigate continuance usage intentions. Departing from this fragmented approach, this study adopts a stage-based perspective to examine how individuals’ adoption of MaaS differs across three distinct phases, including pre-adoption, onboarding, and post-adoption, based on cross-sectional comparisons of users with different levels of experience. We developed structural equation models aimed at three different stages by integrating several theoretical frameworks from consumer marketing, including the theory of planned behavior, the technology acceptance model, and customer satisfaction theory. Using questionnaire data from Beijing, we found stage-specific factors and mechanisms that influence MaaS use, particularly the differential influencing patterns of carbon credit incentives over time. The findings demonstrate that: (1) At the pre-adoption stage, subjective norms, environmental awareness, and carbon credit incentives positively influence intentions to MaaS adoption, while perceived privacy risk and habit have no significant direct effects. (2) During the onboarding stage, perceived usefulness emerges as the central contributor. Personal innovativeness and perceived ease of use influence perceived usefulness indirectly. (3) At the post-adoption stage, satisfaction and service quality are the primary determinants of MaaS continuance use, while carbon credit incentives have no direct effect. (4) Carbon credit incentives function as a direct motivator in the pre-adoption stage but transition to a fully mediated role in later stages. These results demonstrate that as users become more engaged with MaaS, carbon credit incentives shift from directly activating behavior to indirectly facilitating it through cognitive and affective mediators. The study provides substantial empirical evidence to inform the design of tailored promotional strategies for MaaS platforms and policy interventions in consumers’ use intention for MaaS during different stages.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Assessing stakeholder impacts of capacity regulations and algorithmic capacity-on-demand mechanisms in European air traffic management: A network-level ECAC operational case study
Authors: Alfons ­Borràs, César ­Trapote-Barreira
Abstract: Regulatory mechanisms in European air traffic management, including Air Traffic Flow Management slot allocation and flow restrictions, are widely used to address sector-level demand-capacity imbalances. Although effective for safety and feasibility, they impose departure delays that propagate through airline rotations, increasing costs, reducing passenger reliability, and disrupting airport operations. Standard Air Traffic Flow and Capacity Management assessments mainly report regulation compliance and aggregate delay, without explicitly assessing network propagation or differentiated stakeholder impacts. This paper compares the regulatory baseline with an algorithmic demand-capacity balancing approach based on early delegation of clusters of aircraft to adjacent sectors. Under congestion, control of eligible aircraft is proactively reassigned to reshape sector occupancy profiles and balance workload across neighboring sectors, without changing traffic demand or declared capacities. A stakeholder-oriented framework evaluates impacts on airlines, passengers, airports, and air navigation service providers, combining monetized indicators with proxy metrics where valuation is not feasible. Results indicate that early delegation substantially reduces the need for sector-level Air Traffic Controller capacity regulations, lowering direct and reactionary delay and associated costs. Reduced delay propagation is associated with more stable schedules and a smoother temporal distribution of demand for airport infrastructure and services. Overall, rigid regulation-driven allocation can create system-level inefficiencies even when safety constraints are satisfied. Adaptive, data-driven balancing mechanisms show potential to improve efficiency and to alter the distribution of congestion-related impacts, informing policy discussions on the evolution of demand-capacity management in European air traffic systems.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Exploring factors influencing speeding patterns with connected vehicle data for road context-sensitive policy implications
Authors: Yeeun Kim, Mohamed Abdel-Aty, Uibeom Chun
Abstract: Speeding is a major risk factor for traffic safety, but how it should be measured and analyzed remains limited in two respects. First, prior studies have largely relied on average speeds or binary speeding indicators, which obscure how the intensity of speeding is distributed. Second, road environment effects are often treated as uniform, without accounting for how the same feature may operate differently depending on the broader roadway setting. This study addresses both gaps by examining how road environment factors shape the compositional structure of speeding, that is, the relative proportions of different speeding levels, and by modeling these effects separately across different road settings. Using connected vehicle trajectory data from Central Florida, speeding was classified into four ordinal levels: incidental, ordinary-mild, ordinary-moderate, and severe. Dirichlet regression models were developed to analyze the influence of road environment features, including the built environment, greenery, land use, and roadway design, across three distinct contexts: suburban commercial, suburban residential, and urban general. The results show that road environment features act as a behavioral cue that draws drivers toward specific speeding intensities, and that the same feature can do so differently depending on the road context. These findings underscore the need for context-sensitive speed management and provide a basis for targeted policy recommendations to mitigate higher-intensity speeding.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Tactical parking enforcement planning: Optimizing resource allocation under driver response
Authors: Mohsen Yahyaei, Michel Gendreau, Nikolaj Van Omme
Abstract: Municipal parking enforcement shapes driver compliance, equity, and revenue, yet most analytical models emphasize local equilibria or operational routing rather than the tactical allocation of resources across heterogeneous regions. We develop an integrated behavioral–optimization framework linking enforcement intensity, driver choice, and revenue. Using the Lambert–W function, we derive a closed-form critical staffing threshold n⋆ that delineates the transition from weak to effective deterrence. This behavioral mechanism is embedded in a dynamic program that allocates limited patrol units across regions while enforcing a uniform minimum detection-probability constraint as an equity requirement. Computational experiments on synthetic city archetypes and a six-region case study show that (i) moderate fines and balanced staffing maximize long-run revenue, (ii) overstaffing and excessively high fines yield diminishing returns, (iii) technology that raises detection efficiency can maintain deterrence with fewer officers, and (iv) equity constraints reallocate resources toward underserved areas at modest fiscal cost. The framework provides a tractable, data-informed basis for setting staffing, fines, and technology investments that unifies behavioral deterrence with tactical enforcement planning.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Profit-aware graph framework for cross-platform ride-sharing: Analyzing allocation mechanisms and efficiency gains
Authors: Xin Dong, Jose Ventura, Vikash V. Gayah
Abstract: Ride-sharing has the potential to reduce travel costs and VMT by increasing vehicle occupancy. However, fragmentation across competing ride-hailing companies confines shared trips within individual platforms, limiting system-wide efficiency gains. Overcoming this barrier requires fair and incentive-compatible profit allocation mechanisms. This study proposes a profit-aware collaborative framework to evaluate how collaboration under different profit allocation mechanisms influences the feasibility and performance of cross-platform ride-sharing. The proposed framework embeds profit-aware constraints directly into the rider matching process. This allows profit considerations to shape feasible cross-platform matches while ensuring that collaboration remains beneficial for all participating platforms. Within this framework, we evaluate three representative allocation mechanisms—equal-profit-based, market-share-based, and Shapley-value-based—through large-scale simulations calibrated to realistic conditions. Results indicate that collaboration improves system efficiency, including higher share rates, reduced waiting times, and lower VMT. Among the evaluated mechanisms, the Shapley-value-based allocation achieves the most balanced improvements in overall system performance and platform profits. We further find that efficiency gains increase with demand density, reflecting economies of scale (EOS) in shared mobility systems, although marginal benefits diminish as sharing opportunities become saturated. These findings provide quantitative insights into how profit-sharing design can support sustainable cross-platform collaboration and improve urban mobility efficiency in increasingly competitive ride-hailing markets.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Fiscally regressive subsidies and the spatial diffusion of electric vehicles in French cities
Authors: Marie Holzer, Marco Percoco
Abstract: This paper investigates the equity implications of the 2018 policy change regarding France’s electric vehicle (EV) subsidies, focusing on its differential impact across French municipalities (i.e., communes) with varying income levels. Using a synthetic event study and a synthetic difference-in-differences approach, a significant and disproportionately lower rate of EV fleet growth is identified in communes with higher shares of non-taxable (i.e., lower-income) households. Although the nominal subsidy reduction for new EV purchases was the same (€1,500), the proportional financial burden was larger for lower-income households, thus inhibiting EV uptake in communes with larger shares of non-taxable households. Robustness checks—including placebo tests, alternative treatment definitions, and the exclusion of outlier years and regions—support the validity of the causal inference. Additionally, the results show that the €1,000 additional benefit for non-taxable households on secondhand vehicles did not sufficiently offset the impact of the reduction in new EVs. These findings underscore the regressive effects of uniform subsidy cuts across communes with different income levels, which may hinder lower-income households from participating equally in the clean energy transition. This work contributes to the literature on environmental equity of financial incentive policies and offers policy-relevant insights for designing socially inclusive decarbonization strategies amid declining public subsidies across Europe.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Does the integrated fare policy strengthen the synergy between micromobility and mass public transit: A multimodal travel pattern analysis in Seoul
Authors: Sooyoung Lim, Zhenlong Li
Abstract: Seoul, South Korea launched the Climate Companion Card in 2024, a citywide integrated fare that offers unlimited subway and bus travel with an option to include the public shared bicycle. The policy was designed to strengthen micromobility–transit pairing for first- and last-mile trips. Using a 24-month station-level panel from January-December 2023 and January-December 2024, this study examines how the relationship between shared bicycle demand and nearby public transit intensity changed during the policy period. We combine spatial econometric models with station fixed-effects panel models and month-specific interaction profiles. The spatial models show that shared bicycle demand remains strongly clustered across nearby stations and that neighboring transit-rich areas exert competitive pressure on local bicycle demand. The fixed-effects estimates indicate a negative post-policy shift in the subway-bicycle linkage for both origin and destination demand. Month-specific estimates confirm that this weaker linkage is not driven by a single month, although individual monthly estimates remain imprecise. Overall, the findings suggest that fare integration alone did not uniformly strengthen micromobility–transit connections in Seoul.
Journal: Transportation Research Part A: Policy and Practice

Title: Impacts of new public transportation stops on bike-sharing demand: A counterfactual analysis using SeoulBike data
Authors: Su-Yeon Kim, Yoon-Bin Cho, Do-Hyeon Ryu
Abstract: Bike-sharing offers a flexible and accessible mode of transportation, particularly for short-distance travel before or after using public transit as a “first-mile” or “last-mile” solution. As a fundamental component of integrated urban mobility systems, bike-sharing enhances multimodal connectivity and complements pedestrian accessibility. Given their integration with transit systems, the installation of new public transportation stops can influence bike-sharing demand in complex ways. This study quantifies these impacts through counterfactual analysis using the Bayesian Structural Time Series model. Rental and return data from SeoulBike, covering 2,843 stations from September 2015 to December 2025, are analyzed to compare actual and predicted demand under a hypothetical scenario in which new transit stops had not been installed. The resulting impacts are classified into three categories: relative increase, relative decrease, and no significant change. Although overall trends indicate a general increase in demand, certain locations exhibit decreased usage, suggesting that the complementary or substitutive relationship between transit and bike-sharing varies across local contexts. A supplementary analysis employs geographically weighted regression to quantitatively assess how land use characteristics shape variations in bike-sharing demand. The model captures spatial heterogeneity by examining the influence of commercial, residential, industrial, and green areas, as well as the density of nearby bus and subway stops.
